newsitem.title: FRANCE: Arthuis seeks informal EU stability council - report.
newsitem.headline: Arthuis seeks informal EU stability council - report.

text.p: French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said in a newspaper interview that he would push for the creation of an "informal" stability council to coordinate economic policies of European countries with a single currency.
In an interview in Monday's Les Echos, Arthuis said he envisaged "an informal council, like the Group of Seven, whose members would be only the euro countries."
An advance copy of the interview was sent to Reuters.
"For the moment, I don't have a consensus. But I'm counting on enlarging the circle of adherents," Arthuis said. Earlier this month he said he had German backing for the proposal.
"The central bank of Europe will have, at the institutional level, in complete independence, the same prerogatives as our Bank of France -- guarding over price stability," Arthuis said.

"But exchange rate policy remains the responsibility of the states. This prerogative should be exercised by the ECOFIN (council of European finance and economy ministers) but will be debated first among euro member countries, within the stability council," he said.

Arthuis said he hoped European Union leaders meeting in Dublin this month would succeed in striking a three-part agreement on "the legal status of the euro; an exchange rate system between the euro and currencies of EU countries in line to join;...and, finally, the stability pact."
The proposed budget stability pact is aimed at preventing countries belonging to a monetary union from running up big deficits after the euro is introduced in 1999.
Arthuis reiterated that France sought a "pragmatic" approach to define the circumstances that would exempt countries from sanctions under the stability pact.
"On this point, we favor a pragmatic approach taking into account the objective situations of each country. The difficulty is to quantify them," he said.

"The (Maastricht) treaty states that, once public deficits exceed three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), countries are considered to have excessive public deficits and are subject to sanctions, barring temporary and exceptional circumstances. Those remain to be identified," he said.

"Beyond two percent recession, we are certainly in an exceptional situation. And if a country under those circumstances has a deficit exceeding three percent of GDP, it shouldn't be declared excessive," he said.

"But if recession is just under two percent, then would such a deficit automatically be excessive? France's position is simple and clear -- it's up to the council to decide, on a case by case basis. It would be a political decision," he said.
EU ministers earlier this month failed to agree on the terms of the stability pact because Germany insisted on having the circumstances quantified.
